name: IPv6 Addressing
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Read, compress, and classify IPv6 addresses, build EUI-64 IDs, explain SLAAC and NDP, and configure IPv6 on a Cisco router.

lesson.intro: IPv6 looks intimidating mostly because of its notation. Underneath are a few rules: how to shorten and expand an address, which leading digits mean which type, how a host builds its own address, and the commands that enable it in IOS.
objectives: Compress and expand IPv6 addresses with the two rules
Find the prefix of an IPv6 address and explain the /64 convention
Classify global unicast, unique local, link-local, multicast and anycast addresses
Build a modified EUI-64 interface ID and explain SLAAC, DHCPv6 and NDP
Configure and verify IPv6 on a Cisco router interface

sections.title: Why IPv6, and what an address looks like
sections.key: An IPv6 address is 128 bits written as eight 16-bit hextets of four hex digits, and IPv6 drops broadcast, replaces ARP with NDP and lets hosts configure themselves.
sections.body:
IANA handed out its last IPv4 blocks in 2011. NAT bought decades, but hosts behind NAT are hard to reach and every translation adds state. **IPv6** is the real fix.

An IPv6 address is **128 bits**: 2^128, about 3.4 x 10^38 addresses. One standard LAN (a /64) holds 2^64, the whole IPv4 space squared.

It is written in **hexadecimal**, each digit 4 bits, as **eight groups of four hex digits** separated by colons. Each 16-bit group is a **hextet** (Odom says quartet). Hex is not case-sensitive; IOS displays uppercase.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Most networks run **dual stack**: interfaces carry IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, and hosts prefer IPv6 when both work.

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: One hextet: 0db8
visual.caption: Each hex digit is 4 bits: 0 = 0000, d = 1101, b = 1011, 8 = 1000.

visual.title: What else IPv6 changes
rows: Jobs that used broadcast use multicast
Neighbor Discovery (part of ICMPv6) finds MACs and routers
Hosts build their own address from a router advertisement (SLAAC)
Every device can have a globally unique address
A fixed 40-byte header makes forwarding cheaper

sections.deeper: Hex digits to binary, for reference: 0 0000, 1 0001, 2 0010, 3 0011, 4 0100, 5 0101, 6 0110, 7 0111, 8 1000, 9 1001, a 1010 (10), b 1011 (11), c 1100 (12), d 1101 (13), e 1110 (14), f 1111 (15). You need these for EUI-64 and for prefixes that end in the middle of a hextet.
sections.tip: 2001:db8::/32 is reserved for documentation, which is why it fills books and exam questions. Real global prefixes come from your ISP or registry.
sections.pitfall: Treating IPv6 groups like IPv4 octets. Each group is 16 bits (four hex digits), so there are 8 groups, and each hex digit is 4 bits.

check.question: How many bits does one hextet (one colon-separated group of four hex digits) hold?
check.explanation: Four hex digits at 4 bits each make 16 bits, and eight hextets make 128 bits. 8 bits is an IPv4 octet, and 4 bits is a single hex digit.

sections.title: Shortening and expanding addresses
sections.key: Shorten an IPv6 address by dropping leading zeros in each hextet, then replacing one run of two or more all-zero hextets with ::, only once.
sections.body:
Typing 32 hex digits is slow and error-prone, and routers always display the short form, so read it fluently.

**Rule 1: drop leading zeros in each hextet.** 0db8 becomes db8 and 0000 becomes 0. Only leading zeros go: ff00 stays ff00.

**Rule 2: replace one run of two or more all-zero hextets with ::.** Use :: only **once**: twice, nobody could tell how many zeros each stands for. Compress the longest run; on a tie, the first (RFC 5952). A single zero hextet stays 0.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

**Expanding** reverses this: pad each hextet to four digits, then turn :: into enough 0000 groups to make eight.

[[visual 3]]

`::` alone is the unspecified address, `::1` is loopback, and :: may start or end an address (fe80::1, 2001:db8:1:2::).

steps.label: Rule 2 on the run of three zeros

visual.title: fe00:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:0000:0056
rows: Rule 1: leading zeros gone, fe00 kept whole
Rule 2: the longest run (3 hextets) becomes ::. Shortest
**Wrong**: dropped the trailing zeros of fe00

sections.pitfall: Removing trailing zeros. In fe00 or 2a00 the zeros are trailing and must stay; only leading zeros in a hextet can be dropped.

activity.title: Compress and expand
activity.prompt: Compress five addresses. Before you check each one, say which run of zero hextets you will replace with :: and why. Then expand one back to all 32 hex digits and confirm you end up with exactly eight hextets.

check.question: Which is the shortest valid form of 2001:0db8:0000:0001:0000:0000:0000:0001?
check.explanation: Drop leading zeros, then compress the longest zero run (hextets 5 to 7) into :: to get 2001:db8:0:1::1. Compressing the single zero hextet instead is longer, and ::1::1 uses :: twice, which is illegal.

sections.title: Compression drills: five addresses, five traps
sections.key: Apply rule 1 to every hextet first, then compress only the longest run of two or more zero hextets; expanded, an address always has 8 hextets and 32 hex digits.
sections.body:
Exam questions on IPv6 notation each hide one trap. Work these five yourself before reading the answers. For each, drop leading zeros in every hextet first, then look for the longest run of two or more 0 hextets.

[[visual]]

Canonical text is lowercase (IOS still displays uppercase). Writing 2001:db8:1::1:0:1:0 is legal but not canonical, because :: should not replace a single hextet.

Expanding works in reverse: 2001:db8:a0:: shows three hextets, so :: stands for five zero hextets, and a0 pads to 00a0. Self-check: exactly eight hextets and 32 hex digits.

steps.label: Trailing run
steps.note: The four zeros at the end become `::`, and the single 0 stays

steps.label: No run long enough
steps.note: Every zero hextet stands alone, so no `::`

steps.label: Two runs
steps.note: The four-hextet run beats the two-hextet run

sections.tip: Do rule 1 on every hextet before you look for zero runs. It turns 0000 into 0 and makes the runs easy to see and count.
sections.pitfall: Shortening 0010 to 1 or 00a0 to a. Only leading zeros go: 0010 is 10 and 00a0 is a0.

check.question: What is the shortest valid form of 3001:0000:0000:0bad:0000:0000:0000:0000?
check.explanation: Both zero runs could be compressed, but only once, and the longer run (four hextets at the end) gives the shortest result: 3001:0:0:bad::. Using :: twice, as in 3001::bad::, is illegal.

sections.title: Prefixes and the /64 convention
sections.key: Nearly every IPv6 LAN is a /64: a routing prefix (often /48), a 16-bit subnet ID counted in hex, and a 64-bit interface ID that identifies the host.
sections.body:
IPv6 writes the network and host split as a prefix length after a slash, like IPv4 CIDR. There are no dotted masks.

[[visual]]

To find an address's prefix, keep the bits the prefix covers and zero the rest. On a hextet boundary (/16, /32, /48, /64), keep that many hextets: 2001:db8:acad:10:20c:29ff:fe12:3456 is in 2001:db8:acad:10::/64. Otherwise count hex digits, 4 bits each:

[[visual 2]]

Why /64? SLAAC and EUI-64 build a 64-bit interface ID, so the prefix must leave exactly 64 bits. No LAN runs out of hosts, so IPv6 design is about choosing subnet IDs, which you count in hex:

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: 2001:db8:acad:10:20c:29ff:fe12:3456/64
visual.caption: A /48 site has 16 subnet bits: 65,536 /64 subnets.

steps.label: Keep 2 more digits, zero the rest

visual.title: Splitting 2001:db8:acad::/48 into /64s
visual.caption: Other lengths: /48 or /56 for a site, /127 on some router links (RFC 6164), /128 for one address such as a loopback.

sections.pitfall: Zeroing whole hextets for a prefix that ends mid-hextet. A /56 ends after the second hex digit of the fourth hextet, so 2a3c becomes 2a00, not 0000 and not 2a3c.

check.question: A site has 2001:db8:5::/48 and uses /64 LAN subnets. How many subnets can it create?
check.explanation: From /48 to /64 is 16 subnet bits, and 2^16 = 65,536. 2^64 is the number of interface IDs in each /64, not the number of subnets.

sections.title: Unicast address types
sections.key: Classify by the first hex digits: 2 or 3 is global unicast, fd unique local (private), fe80 link-local, ff multicast; ::1 is loopback and :: unspecified.
sections.body:
Configure one address on a router interface and `show ipv6 interface brief` lists two: yours, starting with 2001, and one starting with FE80. Both are **unicast**, with very different jobs.

[[visual]]

**Global unicast** is IPv6's public address. **Unique local** is its RFC 1918: a random 40-bit global ID makes collisions unlikely if two organizations ever connect.

[[visual 2]]

**Link-local** addresses appear automatically on every IPv6 interface and are never forwarded. NDP uses them, routing protocols use them as next hops, and hosts use the router's link-local address as their **default gateway**. In practice they begin fe80:0000:0000:0000, and a router may reuse fe80::1 on every interface.

visual.title: Unique local address
visual.caption: fd plus the 40-bit ID gives the organization a /48.

sections.deeper: Older material mentions **site-local** addresses (fec0::/10). They were deprecated in 2004 and replaced by unique local addresses. The unspecified address :: is used as a source by a host that has no address yet, for example while it runs duplicate address detection on its first address.
sections.pitfall: Dismissing fe80 addresses because they are not routable. Link-local addresses run IPv6's control plane: neighbor and router discovery, routing protocol next hops and the hosts' default gateway.

check.question: A host shows the address fd4c:2a1b:93e0:10::25. What type of address is it?
check.explanation: Addresses beginning with fd come from fc00::/7, the unique local (private) range. Global unicast begins with 2 or 3, link-local with fe80, and multicast with ff.

sections.title: Multicast, anycast, and no broadcast
sections.key: IPv6 has no broadcast: multicast groups such as ff02::1 and ff02::2, and each address's solicited-node group (ff02::1:ff plus its last 24 bits), do that work.
sections.body:
An IPv4 ARP request interrupts every host on the VLAN, although only one owns the address. IPv6 removes broadcast. Messages for several devices go to a **multicast** group (ff00::/8), and only members process them. The fourth hex digit is the **scope**: ff02 link-local (never routed), ff05 site, ff08 organization, ff0e global.

[[visual]]

Every unicast address has a **solicited-node** group. NDP asks for a MAC there, so only hosts whose addresses end in the same six hex digits even look:

[[visual 2]]

**Anycast** puts the same unicast address on several devices (`ipv6 address 2001:db8:1:2::99/128 anycast`); routing delivers each packet to the nearest. It has no special range; DNS root servers are the famous example.

visual.title: Link-local multicast groups
rows: All nodes on the link (closest thing to broadcast)
All routers on the link; hosts send RS here

steps.label: Take the last 24 bits (6 hex digits)

sections.pitfall: Saying IPv6 uses broadcast to find neighbors. IPv6 has no broadcast at all; NDP uses solicited-node multicast and ff02::1 instead.

check.question: What is the solicited-node multicast address for 2001:db8:0:12::1?
check.explanation: Take ff02::1:ff and append the last six hex digits of the unicast address (00:0001), giving ff02::1:ff00:1. ff02::1 is all nodes, and ff05 would be site scope.

sections.title: Modified EUI-64
sections.key: Modified EUI-64 builds a 64-bit interface ID from a MAC: split the MAC in half, insert fffe, and flip the seventh bit, which changes the second hex digit by 2.
sections.body:
Configure `ipv6 address 2001:db8:1:1::/64 eui-64` and the router fills in the last 64 bits from its own MAC. Do the **modified EUI-64** rules by hand:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

The flip only changes the **second hex digit**, always by 2:

[[visual 3]]

Cisco routers build their automatic link-local addresses the same way: fe80:: plus the EUI-64 ID, so ff:fe in the middle reveals a MAC. Many PCs use random IDs for privacy. Typing a full address with `eui-64` keeps only the prefix.

[[visual 4]]

steps.label: Flip the 7th bit of the first byte

visual.title: Second hex digit after the flip
visual.caption: So 00 gives 02, 02 gives 00, 16 gives 14, 30 gives 32.

visual.title: Three more
visual.caption: 0d29 splits into 0dff (shortened to dff); 00ff shortens to ff.

sections.pitfall: Forgetting the bit flip. MAC 0013.1234.abcd does not become 0013:12ff:fe34:abcd; the seventh bit must be inverted, giving 0213:12ff:fe34:abcd.

activity.title: Build EUI-64 interface IDs
activity.prompt: Use the EUI-64 builder with a MAC that starts with 00, then one that starts with 02. Predict the second hex digit of each interface ID before you look, and notice exactly where fffe lands.

check.question: What modified EUI-64 interface ID does MAC 30f7.0d29.8568 produce?
check.explanation: Split into 30f70d and 298568, insert fffe to get 30f70dfffe298568, and flip the seventh bit of 30 (0011 0000 becomes 0011 0010, which is 32). Grouped and shortened: 32f7:dff:fe29:8568. The first choice skips the flip, and the others put fffe in the wrong place.

sections.title: SLAAC, DHCPv6, and NDP
sections.key: NDP (part of ICMPv6) replaces ARP and finds routers; hosts get addresses by SLAAC or DHCPv6, but always learn the default gateway from the router advertisement.
sections.body:
Plug a laptop into an IPv6 LAN and within a second it has a global address and a gateway, with no DHCP server. That is **NDP** (Neighbor Discovery Protocol) at work.

[[visual]]

**Duplicate Address Detection (DAD)** reuses NS and NA: before using any address, a host sends an NS for it; an NA in reply means a duplicate.

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

Cisco RAs have both flags off by default, so hosts use SLAAC. A router interface can be a client too (`ipv6 address autoconfig` or `ipv6 address dhcp`), and `ipv6 dhcp relay destination` relays to a remote DHCPv6 server, like `ip helper-address`.

visual.title: NDP messages
rows: A host asks routers to identify themselves
Prefix, length, flags; its link-local source becomes the gateway
Asks for a MAC: replaces the ARP request; also DAD
Carries the MAC: replaces the ARP reply
Points to a better first hop
visual.caption: Results go in the neighbor table: `show ipv6 neighbors`.

messages.label: DAD on the new address, then use it

visual.title: Three ways to get an address
visual.caption: In all three the default gateway is the router's link-local address, from the RA: DHCPv6 has no gateway option.

sections.pitfall: Expecting a stateful DHCPv6 server to hand out the default gateway. DHCPv6 has no gateway option; hosts always learn the gateway from router advertisements.

check.question: Which NDP message does the job of an IPv4 ARP request?
check.explanation: A Neighbor Solicitation asks the owner of an IPv6 address for its MAC address, sent to the target's solicited-node group. The Neighbor Advertisement is the reply, like an ARP reply. RS and RA are about finding routers and prefixes.

sections.title: Configuring and verifying IPv6 on a router
sections.key: IPv6 routing is off by default: enable it with ipv6 unicast-routing, then give each interface an ipv6 address with its prefix length and no shutdown.
sections.body:
R1's G0/0 should use 2001:db8:0:12::1/64. Unlike IPv4, IPv6 routing is **off by default**. Without `ipv6 unicast-routing`, the router accepts addresses but acts like a host: it forwards no IPv6 packets and sends no RAs, so SLAAC hosts never learn a prefix.

[[visual]]

A second `ipv6 address` **adds** an address rather than replacing the first; remove one with `no ipv6 address` and its value.

[[code]]

The link-local here is EUI-64 from MAC 0050.56ab.12cd. FF02::2 is joined only because routing is on, plus one solicited-node group per address.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Commands
rows: Global: turns on IPv6 routing and RAs
Assigns an address; the prefix length goes right on it
Assigns the prefix; the router builds the interface ID
Replaces the automatic link-local (must be in fe80::/10)
Link-local only: enough on router-to-router links

visual.title: Verify
rows: Status in brackets and addresses, including fe80, without prefix lengths
Link-local, each global address with its subnet, joined groups
**C** for the /64 and **L** for the router's own address as a /128
The NDP neighbor table, like the ARP cache

sections.code:
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# interface g0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:0:12::1/64
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ipv6 interface g0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  IPv6 is enabled, link-local address is FE80::250:56FF:FEAB:12CD
  Global unicast address(es):
    2001:DB8:0:12::1, subnet is 2001:DB8:0:12::/64
  Joined group address(es):
    FF02::1
    FF02::2
    FF02::1:FF00:1
    FF02::1:FFAB:12CD
  Hosts use stateless autoconfig for addresses.
sections.tip: Hosts on this LAN use FE80::250:56FF:FEAB:12CD, R1's link-local address from its RAs, as their default gateway.
sections.pitfall: Configuring interface addresses but forgetting ipv6 unicast-routing. Everything looks right in show ipv6 interface brief, yet the router forwards no IPv6 packets and sends no RAs.

activity.title: Lab: IPv6 on a router link
activity.prompt: Enable IPv6 routing, give G0/0 the address 2001:db8:0:12::1/64, and bring the interface up. Then run show ipv6 interface brief and find the fe80 link-local address you never typed. Abbreviations work here just like IPv4 (sh ipv6 int br).

check.question: R1's interfaces already have IPv6 addresses and are up/up. Which command must be added so R1 forwards IPv6 packets between them?
check.explanation: IPv6 routing is off by default; ipv6 unicast-routing in global configuration turns it on. ipv6 enable only adds a link-local address to one interface, and ip routing controls IPv4.

sections.title: Reading IPv6 output and fixing common mistakes
sections.key: Most IPv6 faults leave a fingerprint: compare each address's /64 with its neighbors, and check that ipv6 unicast-routing is on and no stale address lingers.
sections.body:
Most IPv6 trouble tickets come from a short list of mistakes, each with a fingerprint in show output.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

Here G0/0 still carries an old 2001:DB8:0:99::1 that conflicts with another router, and G0/1's link-local, with FF:FE in the middle, was built by EUI-64.

The habit that catches all of these: read each address in `show ipv6 interface brief`, work out its /64, and compare it with the hosts and neighbors on the same link.

visual.title: Mistakes and their fingerprints
rows: Addresses up/up, but no FF02::2 joined and hosts get no SLAAC address
Router 2001:DB8:0:21::1/64, host 2001:db8:0:12::50/64: link-local works, global traffic fails
Compare the first four hextets character by character
Two global addresses on one interface; the old one may conflict
`no ipv6 address` with the old value
No MAC-based fe80 address after `ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local`
DAD found another user; the router does not use it and logs a message
Find the other device with `show ipv6 neighbors`

sections.code:
R1# show ipv6 interface brief
GigabitEthernet0/0     [up/up]
    FE80::1
    2001:DB8:0:10::1
    2001:DB8:0:99::1
GigabitEthernet0/1     [up/up]
    FE80::250:56FF:FEAB:12CD
    2001:DB8:0:21::1
sections.tip: For any IPv6 connectivity question, write down the /64 of each address involved. Most problems are a prefix mismatch or IPv6 routing switched off.
sections.pitfall: Assuming a link-local ping that succeeds proves the global addresses are fine. Link-local works on any shared link regardless of the global prefixes configured.

check.question: R1 G0/1 has 2001:DB8:0:21::1/64. A PC on the same switch was configured with 2001:db8:0:12::50/64 and gateway fe80::1, which is R1's link-local address. Pings to remote networks fail. What is the most likely problem?
choices: The PC's address is in a different /64 (2001:db8:0:12::) from R1's LAN (2001:db8:0:21::)
check.explanation: The digits 12 and 21 are transposed, so the PC sits in a /64 that does not exist on that link. Using the router's link-local address as the gateway is normal; the global prefix is what is wrong.

keyTerms.definition: One 16-bit group of an IPv6 address, written as four hex digits; an address has eight.
Shorthand for one run of two or more all-zero hextets; allowed only once per address.
The host part of an IPv6 address, normally the last 64 bits.
Publicly routable IPv6 unicast address from 2000::/3, starting with 2 or 3.
Private IPv6 range fc00::/7 (fd00::/8 in practice), not routed on the internet.
fe80::/10 address created automatically on every IPv6 interface; never routed, used by NDP and as next hop and default gateway.
ff02::1:ff plus the last 24 bits of a unicast address; the target of neighbor solicitations.
One unicast address configured on several devices; routing delivers each packet to the nearest.
Builds a 64-bit interface ID from a MAC: split it, insert fffe, invert the seventh bit.
Neighbor Discovery Protocol, part of ICMPv6: RS, RA, NS, NA, and Redirect; replaces ARP and finds routers.
Stateless Address Autoconfiguration: a host builds its address from the RA prefix plus its own interface ID.
Stateful assigns addresses (M flag); stateless gives only other settings such as DNS (O flag). Neither gives a gateway.
The leading part of a global unicast address assigned by an ISP or registry, often a /48 for a site.
The bits between the global routing prefix and /64, written in hex, that number a site's /64 subnets.
Duplicate Address Detection: an NS for your own address before using it; any reply means the address is taken.
NDP message from a router carrying the prefix, prefix length, M and O flags, and its link-local address as gateway.

summary: 128 bits in eight hextets; drop leading zeros and replace one run of zero hextets with ::, once.
LANs are /64: routing prefix, subnet ID (counted in hex), 64-bit interface ID.
2 or 3 global unicast, fd unique local, fe80 link-local, ff multicast; ::1 loopback, :: unspecified.
No broadcast: ff02::1, ff02::2 and solicited-node groups (ff02::1:ff + last 24 bits) do the work.
EUI-64: split the MAC, insert fffe, flip the seventh bit. SLAAC, stateless or stateful DHCPv6; the gateway always comes from the RA.
IOS: ipv6 unicast-routing, then ipv6 address prefix/length; troubleshoot by comparing /64s.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a teammate who only knows IPv4 how a laptop plugged into an IPv6 LAN ends up with a global address and a default gateway without any DHCP server: what the router advertises, how the laptop builds and checks its address, which NDP messages replace ARP, and why its gateway is an fe80 address.

questions.question: How long is an IPv6 address?
questions.explanation: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits. The interface ID is usually 64 bits, IPv4 addresses are 32, and MAC addresses are 48.

questions.question: How many hextets (colon-separated groups) are in a full, unabbreviated IPv6 address?
questions.explanation: 128 bits divided into 16-bit hextets gives 8 groups of four hex digits each.

questions.question: Which statements about IPv6 compared with IPv4 are true? Choose three.
choices: Hosts can build their own addresses with SLAAC
NDP replaces ARP for finding MAC addresses
Every IPv6 network needs NAT to reach the internet
questions.explanation: IPv6 uses multicast instead of broadcast, supports SLAAC, and uses NDP (ICMPv6) instead of ARP. Addresses are 128 bits, and the huge address space removes the need for NAT.

questions.question: Write 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329 in its shortest form.
questions.explanation: Drop leading zeros (0db8 to db8, 0042 to 42, 0000 to 0), then replace the three zero hextets with ::. ff00 keeps its trailing zeros.

questions.question: Write FE00:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:0000:0056 in its shortest form.
questions.explanation: After dropping leading zeros you have fe00:0:0:1:0:0:0:56. The run of three zero hextets is longer than the run of two, so it becomes ::. FE00 cannot shrink because its zeros trail.

questions.question: Expand 2001:db8:a::1 to its full form with all 32 hex digits, keeping the colons.
questions.explanation: Four hextets are shown, so :: stands for four zero hextets. Then pad each hextet to four digits: db8 to 0db8, a to 000a, and 1 to 0001.

questions.question: Which are valid ways to write 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:0001? Choose three.
questions.explanation: You may compress either zero run, or neither, but only once. ::1::1 uses :: twice, and 2001:db8::1:1 expands to 2001:db8:0:0:0:0:1:1, a different address.

questions.question: 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:0001 has two equal runs of zero hextets. Which form follows the recommended canonical format (RFC 5952)?
questions.explanation: When two zero runs are the same length, RFC 5952 compresses the first one. 2001:db8:0:0:1::1 is still a valid address, just not the canonical form, and ::1::1 is illegal.

questions.question: Which of these is not a valid IPv6 address?
questions.explanation: 2001:db8::abcd::1 uses :: twice, so the number of zero hextets in each gap is unknown. An address may end in :: (2001:db8:0:1::), and ::1 is the loopback.

questions.question: What is the /64 prefix of 2001:db8:acad:10:20c:29ff:fe12:3456? Include the prefix length.
questions.explanation: A /64 keeps the first four hextets and zeros the interface ID: 2001:db8:acad:10::/64.

questions.question: What is the /56 prefix of 2001:db8:cafe:1234::1? Include the prefix length.
questions.explanation: /56 is 14 hex digits: the first three hextets (12 digits) plus the first two digits of the fourth. So 1234 becomes 1200 and everything after is 0.

questions.question: A site is assigned a /56 prefix. How many /64 subnets can it create?
questions.explanation: From /56 to /64 is 8 subnet bits, and 2^8 = 256. A /48 would give 2^16 = 65,536.

questions.question: Why are IPv6 LAN subnets almost always /64?
choices: Routers cannot route prefixes longer than /64
IPv6 prefixes must be multiples of 32
SLAAC and EUI-64 build a 64-bit interface ID, so the prefix must leave 64 bits
questions.explanation: Autoconfiguration assumes a 64-bit interface ID. Longer prefixes are routable (for example /127 links and /128 host routes), and a /64 holds 2^64 addresses, not 65,536.

questions.question: Match each address to its type.
questions.explanation: Read the leading digits: 2 or 3 is global unicast, fd unique local, fe80 link-local, ff multicast. ::1 is loopback and :: (all zeros) is unspecified.

questions.question: Which prefix identifies IPv6 link-local addresses?
questions.explanation: Link-local addresses come from fe80::/10. fc00::/7 is unique local, ff00::/8 multicast, and 2000::/3 global unicast.

questions.question: Which statements about IPv6 link-local addresses are true? Choose two.
choices: Routers never forward packets addressed to them
They must be unique across the internet
questions.explanation: Link-local addresses are created automatically on every IPv6 interface and are only valid on their link. They only need to be unique on that link, which is why fe80::1 can be reused on every interface of a router.

questions.question: Which IPv6 range plays the role that RFC 1918 private space plays in IPv4?
questions.explanation: Unique local addresses are private and routable inside an organization but not on the internet. Site-local was the original idea but was deprecated, and link-local cannot be routed at all.

questions.question: A unique local prefix is fd followed by a randomly chosen 40-bit global ID. What prefix length does that give the organization?
questions.explanation: fd is 8 bits, plus 40 bits of global ID, is 48 bits. The next 16 bits are the subnet ID, leaving a 64-bit interface ID.

questions.question: Match each multicast address to the group it reaches.
questions.explanation: All of these are link-local scope (ff02), so routers never forward them off the link.

questions.question: What is the solicited-node multicast address for 2001:db8:1::a:12cd? Give the shortest form.
questions.explanation: Expanded, the address ends in 000a:12cd, so its last 24 bits (six hex digits) are 0a:12cd. Append them to ff02::1:ff to get ff02::1:ff0a:12cd.

questions.question: What makes an IPv6 address an anycast address?
choices: It comes from the reserved range ff00::/8
It is delivered to every device that holds it
It starts with fe80 and stays on one link
The same unicast address is configured on several devices, and routing delivers each packet to the nearest one
questions.explanation: Anycast has no special range; it is a unicast address used on several devices (on IOS, with the anycast keyword). Delivery to every member describes multicast, and ff00::/8 is the multicast range.

questions.question: How does IPv6 handle the jobs IPv4 did with broadcast?
choices: With anycast to the nearest router
With multicast to groups such as ff02::1
With unicast to every host in turn
questions.explanation: IPv6 has no broadcast. It uses multicast groups such as all nodes (ff02::1), all routers (ff02::2), and solicited-node groups so only interested devices process each message.

questions.question: An interface with MAC 0013.1234.abcd is configured with ipv6 address 2001:db8:1:1::/64 eui-64. What is its global address, in shortest form?
questions.explanation: Split the MAC (001312 and 34abcd), insert fffe, and flip the seventh bit of 00 to get 02: 0213:12ff:fe34:abcd. Dropping the leading zero gives 2001:db8:1:1:213:12ff:fe34:abcd.

questions.question: Put the steps of building a modified EUI-64 address in order.
items: Invert the seventh bit of the first byte
Append the 64-bit result to the /64 prefix
questions.explanation: The MAC is split, padded with fffe to 64 bits, the universal/local bit is flipped, and the result becomes the interface ID after the prefix.

questions.question: Which hex value sits in the middle of every modified EUI-64 interface ID?
questions.explanation: EUI-64 inserts fffe between the two halves of the MAC, which is why you see ff:fe in the middle of addresses like fe80::213:12ff:fe34:abcd.

questions.question: A MAC address begins with 02. After the EUI-64 seventh-bit flip, what does that first byte become?
questions.explanation: 02 is 0000 0010, and the seventh bit is the 1. Inverting it gives 0000 0000, which is 00. The flip goes both ways: 00 becomes 02 and 02 becomes 00.

questions.question: You are in interface configuration mode for G0/1. Type the command that assigns prefix 2001:db8:0:34::/64 and lets the router build the interface ID from its MAC address.
questions.explanation: The eui-64 keyword tells IOS to calculate the last 64 bits from the interface MAC using modified EUI-64.

questions.question: Match each NDP message to its job.

pairs.right: Host asks routers on the link to identify themselves
Router announces the prefix, prefix length, and itself as gateway
Asks for the MAC of an IPv6 address, like an ARP request
Replies with a MAC address, like an ARP reply

questions.explanation: RS and RA handle router and prefix discovery; NS and NA handle address resolution and duplicate address detection.

questions.question: A host configures itself with SLAAC. Where does it get its default gateway?
choices: From a DHCPv6 server's gateway option
From the router's RA: the gateway is the router's link-local address
From a neighbor solicitation sent to ff02::1
It calculates the gateway with EUI-64
questions.explanation: The router advertisement's source is the router's link-local address, and hosts use it as their default gateway. DHCPv6 has no gateway option at all.

questions.question: A LAN uses stateful DHCPv6. Which statement is true?
choices: Hosts get their address, prefix length, and default gateway all from DHCPv6
Hosts build their address with EUI-64 and get only DNS from DHCPv6
Hosts get their address from the DHCPv6 server but still learn the default gateway from router advertisements
questions.explanation: With the M flag set, hosts request an address from the DHCPv6 server, which tracks leases. DHCPv6 carries no gateway, so hosts still rely on RAs for it. Building the address yourself and getting only DNS from DHCPv6 is stateless DHCPv6.

questions.question: What does stateless DHCPv6 provide to hosts?
choices: Addresses only, with DNS coming from the RA
Other settings such as DNS servers, while hosts still build their addresses with SLAAC
questions.explanation: Stateless DHCPv6 (signaled by the RA's O flag) hands out settings like DNS but no addresses, so no server keeps per-host state. The address comes from SLAAC.

questions.question: Put the steps of a host getting a global address with SLAAC in order.
items: Create a link-local address and check it with DAD
Send a Router Solicitation to ff02::2
Receive a Router Advertisement with the /64 prefix
Build a global address from the prefix plus its own interface ID
Run DAD on the new address, then start using it
questions.explanation: The host needs a working link-local address to talk on the link, then asks for routers, learns the prefix, builds its address, and checks for duplicates before using it.

questions.question: PC1 needs the MAC address of PC2 at 2001:db8:1:1::22. Where does PC1 send its Neighbor Solicitation?
questions.explanation: An NS goes to the solicited-node group built from the target's last 24 bits (00:0022), so only hosts with matching endings process it. That is the efficiency gain over an ARP broadcast.

questions.question: Type the command that shows a router's IPv6 neighbor table, the IPv6 equivalent of the ARP cache.
questions.explanation: show ipv6 neighbors lists each neighbor's IPv6 address, MAC address, state, and interface, learned through NS and NA messages.

questions.question: Type the global configuration command that enables IPv6 routing on a Cisco router.
questions.explanation: IPv6 routing is disabled by default. Without ipv6 unicast-routing the router does not forward IPv6 packets or send router advertisements.

questions.question: In interface configuration mode for G0/0, type the command that assigns 2001:db8:0:12::1 with a /64 prefix.
questions.explanation: IPv6 addresses take the prefix length directly after the address with no space, unlike the IPv4 address-and-mask format.

questions.question: Type the interface command that sets G0/0's link-local address to fe80::1 instead of the automatic one.
questions.explanation: The link-local keyword replaces the EUI-64 link-local address. The address must be in fe80::/10, and it takes no prefix length.

questions.question: Both interfaces below are up/up. PCs on G0/0's LAN never get a SLAAC address, and R1 does not forward IPv6 between G0/0 and G0/1. What is missing?
questions.code:
! Excerpt from show running-config
hostname R1
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:DB8:0:10::1/64
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ipv6 address 2001:DB8:0:12::1/64
choices: A manual link-local address on G0/1
questions.explanation: Without ipv6 unicast-routing, R1 behaves as an IPv6 host: it neither routes nor sends RAs, so SLAAC hosts never learn a prefix. The ipv6 address commands already enable IPv6 and create link-local addresses.

questions.question: Hosts on this LAN learn their default gateway from R1's router advertisements. Which address will they use as the gateway?
questions.code:
R1# show ipv6 interface g0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  IPv6 is enabled, link-local address is FE80::250:56FF:FEAB:12CD
  Global unicast address(es):
    2001:DB8:0:12::1, subnet is 2001:DB8:0:12::/64
  Joined group address(es):
    FF02::1
    FF02::2
    FF02::1:FF00:1
    FF02::1:FFAB:12CD
questions.explanation: RAs are sourced from the router's link-local address, so that is what hosts install as their default gateway. FF02 addresses are multicast groups the interface listens on.

questions.question: R1 has ipv6 unicast-routing enabled, and G0/0 has only 2001:db8:0:12::1/64 plus its automatic link-local address. No routing protocol or DHCPv6 is configured. Which of these groups will show ipv6 interface g0/0 list as joined? Choose three.
questions.explanation: Every IPv6 interface joins all nodes (FF02::1); a routing interface also joins all routers (FF02::2); and each unicast address adds a solicited-node group, FF02::1:FF00:1 for ::1. FF02::1:2 and FF05::1:3 are DHCPv6 relay and server groups that are not in use here.

questions.question: Write 2001:0db8:0000:0abc:0000:0000:0000:0000 in its shortest form.
questions.explanation: Drop leading zeros to get 2001:db8:0:abc:0:0:0:0, then replace the run of four zero hextets at the end with ::. The single 0 before abc cannot be part of that run, so it stays.

questions.question: Write fe80:0000:0000:0000:0a00:27ff:fe4e:0001 in its shortest form.
questions.explanation: The three zero hextets after fe80 become ::. 0a00 loses only its leading zero (a00, not a), and 0001 becomes 1. Result: fe80::a00:27ff:fe4e:1.

questions.question: A site splits 2001:db8:acad::/48 into /64 subnets, numbered from subnet ID 0. What is the 17th subnet? Include the prefix length.
questions.explanation: The 17th subnet has subnet ID 16, and the subnet ID is written in hex in the fourth hextet: 16 decimal is 10 hex. So the 17th subnet is 2001:db8:acad:10::/64, not 2001:db8:acad:16::/64.

questions.question: An interface with MAC 00a0.c9e1.7f22 is configured with ipv6 address 2001:db8:5:9::/64 eui-64. What global address does it get, in shortest form?
questions.explanation: Split the MAC into 00a0c9 and e17f22, insert fffe, and flip the seventh bit of 00 to get 02: 02a0:c9ff:fee1:7f22. Dropping the leading zero gives 2001:db8:5:9:2a0:c9ff:fee1:7f22.

questions.question: Based on the exhibit, hosts on G0/0 sometimes reach a router that no longer exists, and a neighbor router reports a duplicate address. What should be fixed?
questions.code:
R1# show ipv6 interface brief
GigabitEthernet0/0     [up/up]
    FE80::1
    2001:DB8:0:10::1
    2001:DB8:0:99::1
GigabitEthernet0/1     [up/up]
    FE80::250:56FF:FEAB:12CD
    2001:DB8:0:21::1
choices: Remove the extra address 2001:DB8:0:99::1 from G0/0
Change G0/1 to a manual link-local address
Replace FE80::1 on G0/0 with an EUI-64 link-local address
questions.explanation: G0/0 lists two global addresses because a second ipv6 address command added 2001:DB8:0:99::1 instead of replacing the old one. Remove the stale address with no ipv6 address 2001:DB8:0:99::1/64. The EUI-64 link-local on G0/1 and the manual FE80::1 on G0/0 are both normal.
